intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, Sedaghatian type (SMDS), is caused by compound heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the GPX4 gene.

paragraphs.text: Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia is a neonatal lethal form of spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. It is characterized by severe metaphyseal chondrodysplasia with mild limb shortening, platyspondyly, cardiac conduction defects, and central nervous system abnormalities (Smith et al., 2014).

paragraphs.text: Sedaghatian (1980) reported 2 Iranian brothers, born within a year of each other, who had a similar skeletal disorder with severe congenital metaphyseal involvement, mild rhizomelic shortness of the upper limbs, and mild platyspondyly. Both died at 3 days of age of cardiorespiratory insufficiency. Only 1 had laboratory tests before death. These showed low calcium, high phosphorus, and high alkaline phosphatase levels, which were attributed to a renal defect. At autopsy, the same infant had pulmonary, renal, and adrenal hemorrhage, as well as subendocardial myocarditis and myocardial necrosis. The parents were normal and had recently had an affected baby girl. Peeden et al. (1992) noted that 1 of Sedaghatian's patients had cortical necrosis of the kidneys at autopsy and showed 'laciness' of the iliac wings on radiographs. Opitz et al. (1987) noted that 1 of Sedaghatian's patients also had 'microphthalmia, asymmetry of ears, depressed nasal bridge, broad nose, short neck, prominent sternum, and short lower extremities.'

paragraphs.text: Koutouby et al. (2000) reported an infant born to nonconsanguineous Yemeni parents whose radiologic findings were consistent with Sedaghatian-type lethal metaphyseal chondrodysplasia. All previously reported patients had died within 4 days of life, but this patient survived 161 days. The patient underwent extensive investigation, including serum calcium, magnesium, zinc, ammonia, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and parathormone levels; liver and renal function tests; TORCH and metabolic screening; skeletal survey; chromosome studies; muscle enzymes; EEG; and CT and MRI of the brain.

paragraphs.text: English et al. (2006) reported a female infant, born to nonconsanguineous Caucasian parents, who had metaphyseal dysplasia and a neuronal migration abnormality consistent with a diagnosis of Sedaghatian spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. She was hypotonic from birth and had recurrent cyanotic episodes within a few hours of delivery. Brain imaging showed absence of the corpus callosum and marked frontotemporal pachygyria. She developed seizures on day 14 of life and died at 17 days of age. English et al. (2006) suggested that agenesis of the corpus callosum is a novel association of the disorder and that neuronal migration abnormalities can occur in it.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2014) studied 2 unrelated families with Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia as part of the FORGE Canada Consortium. Whole-exome sequencing of an affected girl and her unaffected parents identified 2 rare variants in the GPX4 gene: c.587+5G-A, inherited from the mother, and c.588-8_588-4del, which was de novo (NM_001039848.1). Both variants were predicted to affect splicing. In vitro studies confirmed that the first mutation caused part of exon 4 to be spliced out and the second caused skipping of exon 5. Both resulted in a frameshift and premature truncation of GPX4. In a second family, DNA from the affected child was not available. Sanger sequencing showed that both unaffected parents were heterozygous for the same stop mutation in exon 3 of GPX4 (c.381C-A, Y127X).

checks.explanation: Compound heterozygosity is inferred from two different variants; the 5-bp size follows from the notation.

checks.claim: In vitro studies showed that the GPX4 c.588-8_588-4del deletion caused skipping of exon 5, resulting in a frameshift and premature truncation of GPX4.
checks.evidence_quote: In vitro studies confirmed the mutations spliced out part of exon 4 and skipped exon 5, respectively, with both resulting in a frameshift and premature truncation of GPX4.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2014) studied a family with a child who had Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia. DNA from the child was not available, but Sanger sequencing showed that both unaffected parents were heterozygous for a c.381C-A transversion in exon 3 of the GPX4 gene (NM_001039848.1), resulting in a tyr127-to-ter (Y127X) substitution.

checks.claim: Smith et al. (2014) studied a family with a child who had Sedaghatian-type spondylometaphyseal dysplasia.
checks.evidence_quote: Subsequently, a second child with SSMD was identified

checks.claim: DNA from the affected child in the family studied by Smith et al. (2014) was not available.
checks.evidence_quote: although DNA from the child was not available

checks.claim: Sanger sequencing showed that both unaffected parents of the affected child studied by Smith et al. (2014) were heterozygous for a c.381C-A transversion in exon 3 of GPX4 (NM_001039848.1).
checks.evidence_quote: the two unaffected parents were found by Sanger sequencing to each carry the same heterozygous stop mutation in exon 3 of GPX4, c.381C>A, p.Tyr127* (NM_001039848.1)
checks.explanation: Stated directly; a C>A change is a transversion.

checks.claim: The GPX4 c.381C-A transversion results in a tyr127-to-ter (Y127X) substitution.
checks.explanation: p.Tyr127* is the same as Y127X.
